Mediators are working with Iran and the United States on trying to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz , three regional officials and two U.S. officials told The Associated Press, but major hurdles remain between the sides.
The indirect talks come as the conflict, which is entering its eighth month, has caused global economic damage and badly battered Iran. Multiple efforts to allow safe shipping on one of the world’s most crucial waterways have failed.
The officials divulged that the behind-the-scenes efforts continue even after U.S. President Donald Trump initially said he spurned an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi — who stayed in New York after last week’s gathering of world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly — will meet with Qatari mediators Monday about the latest discussions, Iranian state media reported Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying.
Despite Trump’s often bellicose rhetoric, he is open to pursuing a non-military resolution to the conflict if one can be achieved, a senior U.S. official said.
But the Trump administration will not reach a deal with Tehran until nuclear issues are addressed, another U.S. official said. Trump is willing to grant sanctions relief to Iran, along with the release of some frozen funds, for concrete progress on nuclear issues, and while Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, the sides are far apart on timing and which side makes the first moves, the official said.
All the officials were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity about the behind-the-scenes diplomatic negotiations.
The deal would first reopen the strait and lift the US blockade
Two of the regional officials speaking to the AP confirmed that mediators are working with both sides on a proposal that would include reopening the strait and lifting the U.S. blockade, and then removing sanctions.
According to the draft text being discussed, the strait would reopen in accordance with a separate deal that Iran has been discussing with Oman, on the other side of the strait, and it would include no tolls — something Tehran has pursued. That deal seeks to temporarily manage shipping traffic on what was seen as an international waterway before the war.
One regional official said the U.S. is seeking Iranian concessions on nuclear issues that include allowing inspectors to enter the country. Under the memorandum of understanding the two sides signed in June that collapsed within days, Iran’s nuclear program was meant to be discussed over a 60-day period.
The U.S. officials say the United States is skeptical about whether Iran can be persuaded to ultimately reach Trump’s conditions for a deal and would be serious about any promises it makes, especially after it broke the interim deal by firing on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. officials feel their position is getting stronger as Tehran feels the impact of sanctions.
Iran's latest proposal seeks faster action
While Iran’s latest proposal echoes the June deal, a key difference is speed.
Araghchi told a closed-door meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly last week that Tehran had pitched the deal as benefiting Trump in the midterm elections. Araghchi later told journalists that “the seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan.”
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also planned to meet Araghchi on Monday in a bid to help mediators, U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said.
Both the U.S. and Iran have been hurting economically — the U.S. from high oil prices as Iran attacks ships on the strait, and Tehran from the naval blockade and a growing number of U.S. sanctions that bottle up its oil sales. Brent crude, the international standard, is above $108.
For months, the two sides have been trying to outlast the other, while regional countries endure missile and drone attacks as Tehran claims to target U.S. military assets in the region.
Reflecting Iran's impatience, a rare statement on Monday attributed to the theocracy's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei noted the “painful blows” that enemy forces have received near the strait. “Before long, the Arabian Sea, too, will be rid of them,” the statement added.
Tehran's latest proposal again sought to end the fighting on all fronts, including in Lebanon. But a new front has emerged in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are now perched on another crucial waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. That has further pressured global energy markets.
Iran argues that the Houthis have their own demands, and that their conflict with neighboring Saudi Arabia is separate from the U.S.-Iran war, but Iranian officials said they are willing to help in finding a settlement between the Houthis and the Saudis, one of the officials said.
Price and Lee reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Collin Binkley in Washington and AP Middle East editor Victoria Eastwood contributed to this report.

The Trump administration announced Monday it's scaling back how fuel efficient American carmakers need to make their fleets.
The Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards set average fuel economy levels for carmakers. The revised rules, which were finalized Monday, will now require carmakers to make their new passenger car and truck fleets up to 1% more fuel efficient each year, aiming for an average of 34.9 miles to the gallon in model year 2031.
This is down from Biden-era rules, which required an annual 2% increase in fuel efficiency with a goal of most vehicles getting, on average, 50.4 miles to the gallon by 2031.
The rationale: affordability. Administration officials argue that fuel efficiency technology is expensive, and has helped to drive up the cost of vehicles. They estimate that scaling back the standards will shave about $1,300 off the sticker prices of new cars.
"This administration is delivering relief to families and reviving the beating heart of American manufacturing," said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in an online statement announcing the change.
President Trump weighed in over the weekend on Truth Social : "These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car."
Climate advocates and auto industry observers say the rules change is another step in the Trump administration's efforts to roll back Biden-era climate policies — including cutting the federal tax credit for electric vehicle buyers , delaying federal dollars for a nationwide EV charging program , and striking down federal waivers that let California set its own strict pollution regulations.
In a statement emailed to NPR, Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the Center for Biological Diversity, wrote that rolling back the standards would increase gasoline usage and pollution, "costing consumers at the pump and at the doctor's office."
"Trump is tanking sensible mileage standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who're getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump," he continued.
According to AAA , the national average price for gasoline today is close to $4.50 a gallon, and for diesel, a gallon is hovering close to $6.50, just short of last week's record high.
Easing CAFE standards will hinder the industry's realignment toward more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles, said economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University. "It's very bad in the long term, because it slows progress," she said. "Then we make our auto companies less competitive. We give them less practice in making the cars that both Americans will want in the future and that the rest of the world will want." After all, American carmakers hope to continue selling their cars in foreign markets that may have stricter emissions standards. And a future presidential administration could change the rules again.
CAFE standards have been part of the auto industry for decades. In 1975, during that decade's great oil supply shock, Congress enacted rules that encouraged carmakers to make their fleets more fuel efficient in an effort to reduce Americans' dependency on the Middle East for oil.
Since then, the national conversation about fuel efficiency has changed; the U.S. is now the world's largest oil producer, and many regulatory changes have instead been driven by concerns about climate change. Since the early 2010s, the fuel efficiency requirements for passenger cars and light trucks have consistently risen .
In practice, the Biden-era standards meant carmakers needed to make electric vehicles to balance out their gas guzzlers — otherwise they were subject to a fine.
But the Trump administration dropped that penalty last July as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effectively defanging the Biden-era CAFE standards. In December, the White House proposed scaling them back altogether. Soon after, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened a period of public comment .
In its final rule announcing the change, NHTSA also said it's eliminating the ability of carmakers to trade credits amongst themselves for making electric vehicles — a part of the Biden-era CAFE Standards that Republicans often criticized. This rule allowed automakers to buy credits from EV manufacturers to offset making less fuel-efficient vehicles. This helped them meet their CAFE targets.
In announcing the new change, the administration said lowering the CAFE standards will make cars cheaper.
"Instead of allowing manufacturers to design and produce vehicles they believe their customers will want and need, while spreading real-world fuel economy improvements across their fleets, the system has increasingly led manufacturers to try to fit square vehicle pegs in round classification holes to force the adoption of technologies that do not meet the demands of American families," stated NHTSA in the final rule. "All of this adds inefficiency and cost — pushing even more consumers out of an already unaffordable new car market."
"It's true that the price of new cars has gone up quite a lot," says Helper at Case Western. But she contends that much of that is not because of fuel economy standards. Instead, she says, it's because vehicles have gotten larger, they've faced tariffs and supply chain issues in recent years, and they are often loaded with extras like infotainment systems.
A Consumer Reports analysis from 2023 found that between model years 2003 and 2021, vehicles got about 30% more fuel efficient, but attributed the rise in prices to an industrywide shift toward expensive SUVs, rather than from using more fuel-efficient technologies.
And when it comes to the monthly costs of a new car, there are external factors beyond a carmaker's control — like the cost of an auto loan , which is affected both by the Federal Reserve's benchmark lending rate and by an individual buyer's credit score.
"One of the cruxes of vehicle affordability right now is the average monthly payment getting jacked up, because interest rates are so high," says Ellen Hughes-Cromwick, who spent much of her career as Ford's chief global economist and now studies clean energy as a senior visiting fellow at the center-left Third Way think tank.
Plus, a cut in the sticker price might eventually be offset by spending on gas. If vehicles are less fuel efficient, that means drivers will need to fill up at the pump more often — which is especially salient in a year of high gas prices due to the war in Iran.
For now, American carmakers are stuck in a kind of jam.
On the one hand, Helper said, a rules change that makes it easier for them to sell trucks and SUVs is "good in the short-term, because they make a lot of profits making these giant vehicles," though they are not as popular outside of the U.S.
This new move "allows the U.S. more of a playground in this protected little Galapagos of an ecosystem where no one else is wanting to compete," Helper continued.
But the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade group representing car and light-truck manufacturers that sell vehicles to the U.S. and that includes automakers such as Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, praised the move. "We're still reviewing the final rule, but NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions," said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the alliance, in an emailed statement to NPR.
"The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand. Today's final rule is an appropriate course correction," he continued.

articles.title_zh: Prosecutors reopen investigation into alleged 2024 gang rape at Cornell University
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Why an investigation into alleged frat house gang rape is reopening
New York state prosecutors say they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024.
The woman filed a civil lawsuit on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house at the university.
"Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said Monday.
Cornell University said that while it supported the case being brought before a grand jury, "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false".
The woman, referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in her lawsuit that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine.
Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and was incapable of providing consent.
She said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024.
The lawsuit also contains an image purported to be from a Snapchat fraternity group chat, in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe.
Van Houten said on Monday that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from her statement to authorities did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges.
He said he reached out to Jane Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury.
In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges.
In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Jane Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack. He noted the statement differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit.
"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday.
"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
Van Houten added that Jane Doe's lawyers had never been in touch with him to say her original statement was inaccurate or to ask him to reconsider his decision not to bring charges.
He later acknowledged "the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them".
The BBC has contacted Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. In a statement on Monday obtained by CBS, the BBC's US partner, he said: "In the days following the assault, [Jane Doe] was traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode."
Giuffra said Jane Doe never spoke to anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint, adding: "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations."
"The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognise that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them," he said.
Jane Doe also alleged in her civil lawsuit that Cornell did not protect her nor adequately punish the men involved, alleging they were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays".
Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the incident and the university's handling, the suit states, adding that news of the incident quickly circulated through the school.
In November 2024, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house", saying its campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students."
Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law - which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities.
On Monday, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators.
The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell".
"None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," Cornell said.
Jeremy Saland, an attorney for one of the men named in the lawsuit, denied the allegations.
Saland acknowledged his client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat", but "did nothing else." Saland denied his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine".
The case has received national attention following Doe's lawsuit and the announcement the case would be reopened. Several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, have spoken out about it.

CAFE standards have been part of the auto industry for decades. In 1975, during that decade's great oil supply shock, Congress enacted rules that encouraged carmakers to make their fleets more fuel efficient in an effort to reduce Americans' dependency on the Middle East for oil.
Since then, the national conversation about fuel efficiency has changed; the U.S. is now the world's largest oil producer, and many regulatory changes have instead been driven by concerns about climate change. Since the early 2010s, the fuel efficiency requirements for passenger cars and light trucks have consistently risen .
In practice, the Biden-era standards meant carmakers needed to make electric vehicles to balance out their gas guzzlers — otherwise they were subject to a fine.
But the Trump administration dropped that penalty last July as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effectively defanging the Biden-era CAFE standards. In December, the White House proposed scaling them back altogether. Soon after, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened a period of public comment .
In its final rule announcing the change, NHTSA also said it's eliminating the ability of carmakers to trade credits amongst themselves for making electric vehicles — a part of the Biden-era CAFE Standards that Republicans often criticized. This rule allowed automakers to buy credits from EV manufacturers to offset making less fuel-efficient vehicles. This helped them meet their CAFE targets.
In announcing the new change, the administration said lowering the CAFE standards will make cars cheaper.
"Instead of allowing manufacturers to design and produce vehicles they believe their customers will want and need, while spreading real-world fuel economy improvements across their fleets, the system has increasingly led manufacturers to try to fit square vehicle pegs in round classification holes to force the adoption of technologies that do not meet the demands of American families," stated NHTSA in the final rule. "All of this adds inefficiency and cost — pushing even more consumers out of an already unaffordable new car market."
"It's true that the price of new cars has gone up quite a lot," says Helper at Case Western. But she contends that much of that is not because of fuel economy standards. Instead, she says, it's because vehicles have gotten larger, they've faced tariffs and supply chain issues in recent years, and they are often loaded with extras like infotainment systems.
A Consumer Reports analysis from 2023 found that between model years 2003 and 2021, vehicles got about 30% more fuel efficient, but attributed the rise in prices to an industrywide shift toward expensive SUVs, rather than from using more fuel-efficient technologies.
And when it comes to the monthly costs of a new car, there are external factors beyond a carmaker's control — like the cost of an auto loan , which is affected both by the Federal Reserve's benchmark lending rate and by an individual buyer's credit score.
"One of the cruxes of vehicle affordability right now is the average monthly payment getting jacked up, because interest rates are so high," says Ellen Hughes-Cromwick, who spent much of her career as Ford's chief global economist and now studies clean energy as a senior visiting fellow at the center-left Third Way think tank.
Plus, a cut in the sticker price might eventually be offset by spending on gas. If vehicles are less fuel efficient, that means drivers will need to fill up at the pump more often — which is especially salient in a year of high gas prices due to the war in Iran.
For now, American carmakers are stuck in a kind of jam.
On the one hand, Helper said, a rules change that makes it easier for them to sell trucks and SUVs is "good in the short-term, because they make a lot of profits making these giant vehicles," though they are not as popular outside of the U.S.
This new move "allows the U.S. more of a playground in this protected little Galapagos of an ecosystem where no one else is wanting to compete," Helper continued.
But the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade group representing car and light-truck manufacturers that sell vehicles to the U.S. and that includes automakers such as Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, praised the move. "We're still reviewing the final rule, but NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions," said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the alliance, in an emailed statement to NPR.
"The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand. Today's final rule is an appropriate course correction," he continued.

articles.title_orig: Alito bows out of blockbuster Supreme Court climate case
articles.title_zh: Alito bows out of blockbuster Supreme Court climate case
articles.content_orig:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito , in a surprising reversal, has recused himself from participating in a major climate-change case the Supreme Court is set to hear next week, which involves the oil companies Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy .
Environmental groups had called on Alito, one of the court's six conservative justices, to not participate in the case because of his holdings of stock in oil and gas companies. Alito does not hold stock in Exxon Mobil or Suncor Energy, according to his most recent financial disclosure for 2025.
Alito previously refused to step off the case after the Supreme Court accepted it for consideration earlier this year. However, in 2023, he did not participate in the court's decision not to consider jurisdictional questions raised by the companies in the same case.
The case, known as Suncor Energy (USA) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, is focused on the question of whether federal law precludes claims made under state law seeking damages for injuries allegedly caused by climate change to greenhouse gas emissions.
The case is set to be argued on Oct. 5.
"I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate  in this case," Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, wrote lawyers for the parties in the case, on Monday.
Alito's sudden recusal sets up the possibility of a 4-4 split ruling on the Supreme Court in the case. A tie in a Supreme Court decision leaves in place the lower-court decision that was being appealed.
The case involves a lawsuit by the city of Boulder, Colorado, and its surrounding county, that seeks damages for alleged harms from the effects of global climate change. A trial court denied a motion to dismiss that was filed by Suncor and Exxon, and the Colorado state Supreme Court affirmed that ruling, allowing the suit to head to trial.
If the Supreme Court rules against the oil companies, the case would proceed toward trial.
In May, a Supreme Court spokeswoman told NBC News that Alito would not step aside from the case.
"Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party" involved in the case, the spokeswoman told NBC News at the time.
She added that the Supreme Court's legal counsel had advised Alito that "his recusal is not required," according to NBC.

articles.title_orig: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
articles.title_zh: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
articles.content_orig:
Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing country
"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".
Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.
And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.
China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up.
"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home.
"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."
She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".
Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University â one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full.  "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.
About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently
In Singapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging.
It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.
These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times".
"Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore.
"But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it â that's how you analyse and manage it."
He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.
Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions â uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement â and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.
China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".
Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says
Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air.
"The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.
This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers.
One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."
Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."
Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."
Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures
Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.
Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."
And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.
Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.
They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.
Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.
Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects
Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.
Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.
The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home.
"When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."
About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".
Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.
But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity.
"If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo urges concessions for peace as Ukraine war drags on
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo urges concessions for peace as Ukraine war drags on
articles.content_orig:
France may have a highly secularized culture, but it has given Pope Leo XIV a superstar welcome.
In Paris, around 800,000 lined the Champs-Élysées avenue, some waving Vatican or French flags while others climbed trees or stood on each other’s shoulders to get a glimpse of the popemobile. In Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, around 150,000 attended an open-air papal Mass, according to Vatican estimates which dwarf the numbers of faithful who turned out for the last papal visit in 2008.
During the four-day visit, Leo appeared comfortable and relaxed, delivering most of his speeches and reflections in French, as the Chicago-born pontiff sought to tackle several themes during the trip.
A strong focus of Leo’s has been on trying to revitalize faith in a traditional European Catholic heartland as well as on addressing the clerical sexual abuse scandal and big political topics such as artificial intelligence. He’s also offered some more personal, unscripted remarks, helping to shape a clearer picture of himself.
While his predecessor never made official visits to the major Catholic European countries of France and Spain, Pope Leo has traveled to both within the first year and a half since his election.
France is sometimes described as the “eldest daughter of the church” because of its deep Catholic roots, but it’s also faced a long-term trend of declining church attendance with estimates of just 5-8% of the population heading to the pews each week.
French bishops have more recently reported some good news though: a surprising rise in new church entrants after around 8,200 adolescents and 13,200 adults were baptized in 2026. That’s a 20% increase on the year prior, with the church also saying 42% of the adults seeking baptism are aged 18-25, a reflection of a trend showing Gen Z’s openness to religious faith .
It’s something Pope Leo will have noted at the Stade de France when 80,000 young people packed the venue for a jubilant – and loud – prayer vigil. It was similar to when the pontiff visited Spain in June.
“There is a quest for meaning. People need and are in search of meaning and answers to the big existential question,” Rev. Benoît Pouzin, a priest in southwest France involved in youth ministry, told CNN.
France has a strict separation between church and state, so each papal visit needs to be carefully navigated. But in a surprising twist, Leo’s Mass in Paris was celebrated on the Place de la Concorde, a site deeply linked to the secular Republic as it’s where the last king of France, Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined. The separation of the church started with the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution.
In another unusual move later in the trip, President Emmanuel Macron also attended a papal Mass in Metz, a city in the northeast, despite criticism in 2023 for doing the same during Pope Francis’ visit.
Many among the crowds also pointed to Leo’s role as the other major US leader on the world stage. It’s hard not to see him as a counterweight to President Donald Trump. In contrast to the Trump administration, the pope has called for stronger guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence, warning against a “paradise of machines” while in Paris.
Pope Leo said he is taking the warnings about Artificial Intelligence’s threat to humanity seriously, and said it is irresponsible for people to sit back and dismiss the risks of AI.
Trump has dismissed the warnings about AI as a “hoax” which he made during a surprise phone call with Jensen Huang, the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, at a summit in Los Angeles.
“I don’t think that that is fake news – as some have said – to try and pause,” Leo XIV said on board the papal plane from Metz to Rome.
Leo, who has expressed a keen interest in artificial intelligence since the start of his papacy, said that he found it “interesting” that Huang had unveiled a new tool to prevent AI agents from operating out of human control.
“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” the Pope said.
The pope devoted his first major theological document to AI earlier this year, warning about the use of AI in warfare and calling for stronger ethical foundation to the development of the technology.
The pope explained that the Vatican had established its own AI commission to understand how to use it, along with the risks and benefits, and that “we need to continue to invite political leaders, the leaders of AI” so they can “look at what is happening already and what could be down the road.”
He explained: “We are trying to continue to promote dialog, study, investigation, to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point where it could destroy humanity.”
“If someone were to ask me, am I in panic mode? No, I’m not, I sleep at night” the pope said, but added: “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.”
“To simply say, oh, it’s not going to happen and close our eyes to it, I think, is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” Leo said.
The pope, who spoke out against the US war in Iran, also wants a more united Europe, a stronger European Union and stronger international cooperation. “Today, relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilized,” the pope said in Metz on Monday. “The value of keeping one’s word is dismissed; instead, people boast of lies and deceit.”
The pope’s speech also praised one of the founders of the European Union, Robert Schuman, for whom there is an ongoing formal cause to make a saint.
Pope Leo XIV has warned against the use of Christianity by far-right political groups, while calling on the church to be active in seeking to prevent extremism. Speaking on board the papal plane, he said that “the combination of these far-right points of view with a certain kind of religion” cannot be considered an “authentic expression of Christianity.”
The pope’s comments came in response to a question about the rise of extremist parties in Germany as he flew back from making a major speech on European Unity at the French-German border.
“We go back to the values of the Gospel [Christian teaching], which are not about hatred and division, but they’re about understanding and compassion,” the pope said.
The American pontiff also responded to Trump’s White House media ban, which includes CNN and other outlets. In answer to a question from CNN, he said he was “very happy that, here, you are all welcome and good coverage, I think, is very important and that we have it all the way around, for everyone.” The response was classic Leo: signaling his support for the press but not wishing to create an unnecessary dispute with the president.
The American pope’s in-flight interactions with journalists were rare, unscripted moments, with his answers often revealing more about his personality. On the flight from Rome to Paris, the pope was asked if he had anything to do with a miraculous recent Chicago White Sox victory, his beloved baseball team. “No comment,” he said before adding with a smile, “Great things happen in Chicago.”
He also recalled childhood memories of watching Fulton Sheen, the American archbishop and broadcaster who was recently declared “blessed,” one step ahead of sainthood, and revealed he’d been practicing his French but was no longer using the Duolingo language app. “It’s fake news!” he said about recent reports. Leo has in the past been spotted using Duolingo to learn German.
Leo isn’t simply vocal about challenges of his homeland. He also voiced concern over assisted dying with France recently approving legislation granting the right to the incurably ill, which is strongly opposed by the Catholic Church. Leo spoke on the subject several times during his visit – most clearly in the “miracle shrine” town of Lourdes, known for drawing many sick and terminally ill pilgrims to its shrine.

articles.title_orig: NFL trade deadline grades: J.J. McCarthy to the Giants
articles.title_zh: NFL trade deadline grades: J.J. McCarthy to the Giants
articles.content_orig:
EAGAN, Minn. â Even something believed to be the best decision can be tremendously difficult.
Such is the case for Vikings General Manager Nolan Teasley and Head Coach Kevin O'Connell in opting to trade J.J. McCarthy to the Giants in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round draft pick.
O'Connell called Monday "a tough day," and Teasley emphasized the human aspect of the transaction in their respective press conferences with Twin Cities media members.
"These types of decisions for me are never easy because the person is important," Teasley said. "I think he was an important person to this organization. I enjoyed my time getting to know J.J. I want the best for him, and I hope he succeeds in the future."
O'Connell noted nothing about the business decision changes the way he feels about McCarthy or the "hopes" he has for the 23-year-old quarterback moving forward. He believes New York â who recently lost starting QB Jaxson Dart for the season to a knee injury â presents a favorable opportunity for McCarthy.
"As I told him, I'll be pulling for him like crazy, to see him go and do well and apply a lot of the things we've talked about over his period of time here," O'Connell said.
He emphasized the amount of time he's spent with McCarthy since the Vikings drafted him 10 th overall in 2024.
"I care about him. I have tremendous respect for him as a player, a person," O'Connell said. "I've just had a chance to spend time with him this morning, which was emotional. Our relationship means a lot to me. I believe it means a lot to him, and I was just really thankful to have that time 1-on-1 with him.
"These situations are never easy. From a standpoint of being the head coach, you understand hard decisions in the NFL. I understand them firsthand, going back a long way for me personally," O'Connell continued. "It's always going to be about the relationship. It's always going to be about investing in all these players so much and understanding their families are involved with that."
Below are additional takeaways from Monday's media sessions with Teasley and O'Connell.
View photos of the Vikings 53-man roster as of Sep. 28, 2026.
1. Timing & return of trade
O'Connell acknowledged the importance of relationships with players and their families while also recognizing the ultimate business of leading a pro team.
"You understand the decisions in the NFL that have to be made in the best interest in the organization," O'Connell said, "and you have a responsibility, and that's why I credit Nolan throughout â¦ just his ability to handle situations with so much tact and thought, always thinking forward on building our team."
Teasley confirmed that McCarthy never requested a trade, but he declined to specify exactly when conversations around a potential transaction began. He did note that this specific situation â timing, scenario and compensation â prompted the trade to happen how and when it did.
"You have to recognize when a different situation or a new opportunity presents itself that it has the opportunity to present better outcomes," Teasley said. "When the situation with the Giants presented itself, we spoke internally â that's coaches, myself, the personnel staff, ownership â everyone came together. Just in terms of where we are and in terms of our roster, where it is currently â¦ and what we might want to do in the future.
"Ultimately, we came to the conclusion that this was the best path forward and the best decision for the Minnesota Vikings," he added.
Teasley later said things "recently came together" to make the trade.
"We got to the point where the return made sense for us now to get an asset that, in all honesty, is going to help us in the future, or it could help us this season," he said. "So to have another asset that can help us continue to build, because the season and this roster [is] going to constantly evolve, and today's another example of that."
2. Exhausted development plan
Considering McCarthy only made 10 starts, O'Connell was asked about the trade through the lens of: Was there anything else that could have been done to bring McCarthy along?
He said the organization emptied the tank in its efforts to develop the 23-year-old.
"We tried to do everything we could to collaborate with a plan for [him] among coaches, among everybody in this building to try to put him in position to develop and grow," the coach said. "And I do think, you know, I do think he did. I do think he did develop and grow.
"And I think he improved. I think he improved this offseason," he added. "But at the same time, you're always going to look inward and look at it [like the] circumstances, they are what they were and are. But what could we have done differently? And J.J. and I talked about that this morning of, you know, like 'Do I wish I took him out of that first preseason game earlier? You know, whatever it may be, like that's where your mind goes, and I think it's a good question."
3. Murray's trajectory & QB room

articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Nolo was on the verge of becoming a major Category 5 storm early Monday as it moved farther away from Hawaii, the National Hurricane Center said. It was expected to continue gaining strength, reaching peak intensity on Monday before gradually weakening.
The storm is forecast to remain well south and southwest of Hawaii's main islands but approach the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument on Tuesday. That's a vast, 582,000-square-mile protected conservation area northwest of Hawaii.
Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 155 mph early Monday, making it a Category 4 storm. Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 35 miles from Nolo's core and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 150 miles.
Nolo was forecast to bring up to 20 inches of rain to the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island. For Maui, 4 to 8 inches were possible. The rest of Hawaii was likely to get 1 to 3 inches, with 5 at most, enough to trigger isolated flooding, forecasters said.
What's more, Nola-generated swells "will be affecting south-facing shores of the main Hawaiian Islands for the next few days. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions," the hurricane center cautioned early Monday.
All state parks on Hawaii's Big Island and on Maui were closed because of the storm, the state's Department of Land and Natural Resources said.
President Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said.
Nolo formed as another storm, Hurricane Polo , continued to swirl in the Pacific, off Mexico's southwestern coast.
The latest storms add to an unusually active season in the Pacific. Earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell brought damaging winds and heavy rain to the western Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, bringing down trees, damaging roads and knocking out power for thousands.
Last month, Hurricane Lala washed away about 100 homes , triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.

articles.title_orig: Arming an adversary: Why Trump’s offer to sell China weapons belies US policy
articles.title_zh: Arming an adversary: Why Trump’s offer to sell China weapons belies US policy
articles.content_orig:
In an offer that baffled most observers, United States President Donald Trump has made a pitch to his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping that has seldom been made in modern history.
Trump’s suggestion that Beijing buy US weapons was another off-script remark that appeared to stray from official policy, prompting the State Department to clarify that Washington has no such plans.
Trump asked Xi “at one point” whether China was interested in procuring US arms, the US envoy to Beijing, David Perdue, said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday. The president reportedly made the suggestion in discussions with Xi about US arms sales to Taiwan , but it was unclear whether that happened during their joint summit last week or at another time.
The comments are all the more striking given Washington’s concerns about Beijing’s support for Iran, as Trump’s ongoing war with Tehran continues.
Analysts were quick to dismiss Trump’s proposal as lacking any strategic logic – not least of all due to the arms embargo the US has imposed on China since 1989.
“Such ‘gambits’ by Donald Trump [are] spontaneous flights of fancy that are not part of any strategy,” Alejandro Reyes, an Asia Pacific policy specialist and professor at the University of Hong Kong, told Al Jazeera.
“It is certainly unusual to suggest to your main strategic rival and adversary [that it] should buy your weapons.”
But experts also said it revealed how Trump views Beijing: through a strictly mercenary framework.
The analysts were in agreement that Trump’s offer was not a serious proposal and possibly even a joke.
US law strictly prohibits arms sales to China and Washington officially identifies Beijing as its primary strategic and economic competitor – so there is no practical policy framework for such a transaction, said Beijing-based analyst Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation.
“It is an off-the-cuff negotiating probe designed to disrupt standard diplomatic scripts, test reactions and create transactional leverage,” Tangen told Al Jazeera.
The US has always viewed China and its military capabilities with concern, citing its Communist Party’s fusion with the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) as a threat. It has accused Beijing of acquiring and diverting the world’s cutting-edge technologies – including through theft – in order to achieve “military dominance”, a US State Department memo states.
“The US officially regards China as a leading national security threat,” said Reyes.
“The Pentagon’s long-term military planning treats China as the ‘sole pacing threat’, meaning that the US military reckons its technological edge, naval capacity and now its AI progress primarily against China’s capabilities and performance.”
Trump’s remarks were therefore a departure from the policy underpinnings of his administration – and that of previous administrations.
“The remark highlights the friction between Trump’s transactional political style and a national security establishment that views China as a systemic rival to be contained,” said Tangen.
Trump’s motivation, he explained, is based on his need to acquire rare earth metals to replenish America’s depleted weapons stockpiles – which have taken a major hit following his ongoing war with Iran. China dominates the world’s rare earth supply chains.
William Yang, a senior analyst on North East Asia at Crisis Group, agreed that Trump views Beijing through a transactional lens – and that his offer held no realistic, strategic thinking.
“This incident reflects Trump’s almost pure transactional view of Washington’s relationship with Beijing,” Yang told Al Jazeera. It’s also in line with the president’s conduct throughout his second term – making remarks that contradict existing US policies, which sow confusion and require clarification later, he added.
History offers few examples of geopolitical rivals striking arms deals, making Trump’s proposal particularly unusual. Yet, there are a handful of precedents.
During World War II, the US’ Lend-Lease Act to Allied countries also included the Soviet Union – as they were driven by a common enemy, Nazi Germany, explained Tangen.
Years later, technological cooperation between the US and China in the late Cold War “was motivated by a shared objective of countering Soviet power and it never involved frontline technology”, he said.
Dov H. Levin, a professor of international relations at the University of Hong Kong, also pointed to the Iran-Contra affair, when in the eighties, the US sent secret weapons transactions to Iran and Nicaragua – which violated the US Congress and the stated public policy of the government at the time.
“I see no US weapon system that the US would plausibly offer China to purchase in the current state of their bilateral relationship,” Levin told Al Jazeera.
Britain sold jet engines to the Soviet Union in 1947 during the early Cold War, said Reyes. Nazi Germany, in turn, sold the Soviet Union an unfinished heavy cruiser in 1940, during their temporary rapprochement, before invading the country the following year, he added.
“These cases show how commercial or strategic interests have sometimes permitted military transactions between countries that were rivals or subsequently became adversaries,” said Reyes.
But Tangen argued that such transactions reflected “temporary alignments born of immediate geopolitical necessity”.
The analysts agreed that the historical examples do not translate to the relationship between China and the US today.
“What distinguishes today’s China-US relationship is that the two countries are directly competing over the strategic balance of power in the Asia Pacific and beyond – and are even said to be heading for inevitable kinetic conflict,” said Reyes.
If Trump genuinely wanted to use US weapons as a bargaining chip with Beijing, there are multiple barriers in his way, not least of all national security constraints, said the analysts.
Selling weapons to Beijing “would potentially compromise US national security, allow China to gain access to advanced US defence technology and further bolster China’s military modernisation efforts,” said Yang.
Additionally, US systems do not align with Beijing’s security architecture, said Tangen.
“The US model is built for global power projection. Platforms like the F-35 combine extreme technological sophistication – such as stealth, sensor fusion and electronic warfare – but depend on an expensive, vulnerable ecosystem of tankers, AWACS, satellites, forward bases and global logistics,” Tangen said.
The Chinese model, meanwhile, is built for regional defence and sovereignty protection, he added.
“Systems like the J-20 [Chinese fighter jet] are integrated into a robust regional framework combining long-range missiles, drones, domestic sensors, satellites and land-based command-and-control, all backed by a massive industrial base capable of high-volume mass production,” said Tangen.
Reyes was blunt in his analysis of Beijing’s need for US arms: “China now produces most of its own weapons. Why would it need to buy American?”
With the two powers gridlocked in competition over AI , rare-earth metals, the question of Taiwan and the Iran war – their race to increase military exports is no exception.
While Trump may have made the weapons proposal to bolster US arms exports, China has no interest in helping a country that sees it as an existential threat, said the analysts.
The US continues to dominate global arms exports, but China is edging its way higher, becoming the world’s fourth biggest exporter, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
Beijing has largely turned to niche markets in the Global South.
“China has carved out a market for affordable drones, combat aircraft and conventional weapons, particularly in Pakistan [and other parts of] Asia, Africa and the Middle East,” said Reyes.

articles.title_zh: Prosecutors are reexamining a Cornell fraternity rape case. Here's what we know
articles.content_orig:
People walk on the campus of Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., in 2024. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
New York prosecutors say they are reopening an investigation into an alleged rape case from 2024 that involved Cornell University students.
This comes after the alleged victim, referred to as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit in the Supreme Court of the State of New York this month. In it, she claims multiple men drugged and brutally raped her for more than four hours at a Cornell fraternity house in October 2024.
In a nine-page statement, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten announced efforts are underway to reexamine the case. Once his office determines appropriate charges, the case will be presented to a grand jury, he said. Van Houten said he has assigned a senior prosecutor, with experience in sex crimes, to start preparations.
Cornell University issued a statement following news that prosecutors are taking another look at the case.
The school said it supports the decision but defended how university officials handled the case two years ago. Kyle Kimball, vice president for university relations at Cornell, said the school "conducted a thorough Title IX investigation" that lasted several months.
No criminal charges were ever filed.
But Cornell said it held a hearing where "a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days," which included testimony from all sides.
At the end of that hearing, expulsions and suspensions were issued. The statement did not specify which individuals faced those consequences.
Kimball continued in the statement: "Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false."
The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity, of which the alleged rapists were members, was banned from the campus two years ago, when details first emerged.
Doe is suing seven alleged rapists, the fraternity, Cornell University and others.
Her attorneys didn't respond to a request for comment before publication.
The case became subject to fierce social media scrutiny following Doe's lawsuit. Van Houten said people have called his office to demand answers as to why the case was never investigated. Others called to insult and threaten, he said.
Van Houten acknowledged the outrage. In defending his office, he said the civil lawsuit's claims differ from the unnamed victim's sworn statement from two years ago.
"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," he wrote. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."
Van Houten added that his office had never been contacted by Doe's attorneys.
"Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision," he said. Van Houten said he reached out to Doe's attorneys to understand "the discrepancy."

President Donald Trump declares that “this is the final battle” in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November’s midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.
The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against “the deep state,” “warmongers,” “globalists,” “Marxists,” “communists,” and “fascists.”
Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023 , but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump’s campaign and fine print saying it was “Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc.” This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday , citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.
A second advert with the same “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN , showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.” This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
A third , which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump’s speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.
The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.
Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said : “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem , who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)
When asked about the “Love Me” ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán . “It’s inappropriate,” Tillis told reporters .
Rep. Thomas Massie , a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the “Final Battle” ad: “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.”
Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the “Love Me” ad’s production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad “does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions.” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: “How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?”
In another Sept. 24 letter , congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the “Love Me” ad should be taken off the air, as it was “the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”
But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, “ public service announcements .” A White House official told TIME Friday that the ads weren’t political, didn’t have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.
A spokesperson instead said that the ads were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda.”
The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is “purely partisan,” “self-aggrandizing,” or “covert.” But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.
Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act , the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren’t. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.
In defense of the “public service announcements,” the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure .)
“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education,’” the Trump White House said. “When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda.’”

articles.title_zh: NFL Week 3 Sunday aftermath: Tyler Loop's heroics, Drake Maye concerns, Brock Purdy's MVP form
articles.content_orig:
Week 3 was all about the nail-biter.
Of Sunday’s 14 games, 12 ended within one score, and most came down to the final play, including Matthew Stafford 's last-second interception to cement the Rams' second-half collapse at Denver in the nightcap.
Let’s run through key storylines in the aftermath of a Sunday that provided a plethora of heart palpitations, including:
But first, we head to Brazil, which hosted an early contender for Game of the Season on Sunday.
Football’s ability to inspire never ceases.
Ravens kicker Tyler Loop rode a rocky path during his rookie campaign, culminating in a season-ending miss in the team’s Week 18 loss to the rival Steelers with the AFC North title (and the accompanying playoff berth) on the line. That pushed 44-yard kick attempt set in motion an offseason of change in Baltimore. Loop fended off questions about his future, keeping his job despite the immense fallout.
A blocked attempt in Week 2’s disappointing loss to the Saints revived questions about the 2025 draft pick. Then, on Sunday in Rio de Janeiro, Loop got his shot to brush away the haze of the past.
After the Ravens' defense bowed up and kept Dallas out of the end zone late in the fourth quarter, seven seconds remained in 31-31 game. Lamar Jackson rocketed a missile that Zay Flowers leaped to snag for a 27-yard gain , with the receiver immediately getting down as Jackson called a timeout with 1 second remaining and the ball now at Dallas' 38-yard line. Loop lined up the 56-yard attempt and calmly banged it through, with CBS Sports' Jim Nantz eloquently calling the game-winning boot “a trio in Rio.”
Ravens players celebrated with their sometimes-maligned kicker as they pulled off a last-second victory despite stumbles along the way.
Loop’s kick on Sunday didn’t erase the previous big miss or guarantee anything about his future. However, it provided oxygen to a flickering flame. That one kick could have revived a career.
"I was saying on the sideline, 'Your legacy starting now,' because I feel like he has been facing adversity," Jackson said of Loop . "I said, 'What a way to start your legacy in Brazil,' and he finished the rest. He did it. Shout out to special teams, shout out to Loop."
Jackson’s part shouldn’t be understated, either. His ability to deliver that late laser over the middle -- without taking too much time -- was pivotal, as was Flowers' snag and haste to get down. The Ravens moved the ball well on Sunday, but they also were stuffed in short-yardage situations several times.
In a young season in Jesse Minter’s first campaign, the 34-31 win showed fortitude: from the defense keeping the Cowboys out of the end zone on their final drive to Jackson making a play to Loop nailing the winner. It’s the type of victory that could propel a team.
The Ravens needed the win in a hotly contested division.
The Steelers' offense showed life in a 30-27 victory over the Bengals, with Aaron Rodgers finally hitting on some deep strikes after two weeks of them falling incomplete. If the Pittsburgh offense can keep splashing plays, and Rodgers isn’t broken in half, the Steelers will be a tough out.
Cincinnati’s defense came back to the pack a bit after an excellent start to the season. That’s not too much of a surprise. That’s not why Cincy lost, however. Special teams issues were the real killer, as the punt crew gave the Steelers extra chances. Joe Burrow still had a shot late, but a final-drive fumble sealed it. It’s a stinging loss to a division rival, but not one that should worry Bengals fans.
The Browns' defense was locked in again to improve Cleveland to 2-1 , stymying Bryce Young and a Panthers offense that had moved the ball well in the first two weeks. Deshaun Watson showed that, when he avoids the big mistake, he can be a net positive for Cleveland and make game-winning plays. That’s new.
The Patriots were pegged to regress in 2026, partly because of their tougher schedule after winning the AFC East. That might be one element of New England's 1-2 start, but it’s far from the story.
The biggest issue isn’t that the Pats are facing teams that make them pay for mistakes; it’s that Drake Maye has regressed to the point that he’s making rookie-level blunders in Year 3. Week 1’s calamitous turnover fest in Seattle has snowballed. Maye has seven giveaways through the first three games of the season, the most by any player in the NFL. His seven turnovers are the most by a Patriots player in the team's first three games of a season over the last 30 years, per NFL Research.
Perhaps he can explain away the embarrassing fumble in Sunday's blowout loss to Jacksonville, saying there was blood on the ball from the center. But there was no excuse for his second-quarter interception in the end zone. It was a ball that should never have been thrown. That’s Maye’s biggest issue right now: He’s not seeing things clearly. Defenses studied his weaknesses all offseason, and he hasn’t adjusted. Until Maye does, more upchucks like Sunday's performance will ensue.
"I think quarterbacks want to make plays,” Vrabel said Monday morning on the Greg Hill Show, via ESPN's Mike Reiss . “I think they want to throw touchdowns. I think sometimes when Greg and I go golfing, we really want to make a good score, right? Sometimes we’re so focused on it, we try to choke the life out of the golf club, and we’re squeezing it so damn tight that the ball has no choice but to go sideways.
"We need to stop trying to choke the life out of every single play. We need to relax. We need to settle in and go play football and not try to force things that aren’t there.”
Gregg Rosenthal, Jourdan Rodrigue and Nick Shook recap the Week 3 matchup between the Raiders and the Saints.
I already noted last week that the way Las Vegas has been winning is different under Klint Kubiak. It feels repeatable.
The defense has been opportunistic, taking advantage of turnovers. Las Vegas had four takeaways in the fourth quarter of its Week 3 win at New Orleans. The Raiders had only three fourth-quarter takeaways in the entire 2025 season, according to NFL Research. It’s also the first time a team has forced at least four fourth-quarter takeaways in a game since the Cowboys in Week 13 of 2022 vs. the Colts. Yes, the Raiders benefited from a controversial fumble call on Tyler Shough . It also takes players creating such opportunities to benefit from them.
Tight end Brock Bowers ’ return was pivotal. Vegas doesn’t win in NOLA without his 10-catch, 116-yard, one-TD performance. Kubiak deployed Bowers all over the formation, in-line and detached, making him a matchup nightmare. Despite Bowers missing the first two games after undergoing a knee procedure, a magical season for the TE appears quite viable, with Kirk Cousins force-feeding his top target. This offense needs one more outside option to be complete.
The Raiders are the darlings of the league right now, and rightfully so. Kubiak has quickly shown he can win in the big chair. His coordinators have been excellent. Cousins has been steady. Playmakers are making plays. But I should point out that the Raiders' opponents are a combined 1-8 through three weeks. The real test comes in next Sunday, when Kansas City visits Las Vegas .
“It’s a great f---ing win,” Raiders star defender Maxx Crosby said postgame in the locker room . "But we’ve got a great f---ing team coming into town. We already know what it is. It’s the f---ing Kansas City Chiefs.
“Enjoy this s--- tonight, take care of your bodies, and we’re f---ing on a warpath to get what we want, men.”
San Francisco 49ers fans should thank their stars for Brock Purdy and Christian McCaffrey -- and pray they don’t succumb to the injury bug that continues to plague the club.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow policy ending medical treatments for transgender inmates
articles.title_zh: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow policy ending medical treatments for transgender inmates
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Trump administration on Monday asked the Supreme Court to revive for now a Bureau of Prisons policy cutting off certain medical interventions and social accommodations for transgender inmates.
The Justice Department's emergency appeal stems from a federal district court order issued last month that continued to prohibit the Bureau of Prisons from enforcing its new rules against any inmate who is or will be diagnosed with gender dysphoria.
The judge overseeing a challenge to the policy, U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, ordered the Trump administration to continue providing medical care to a class of transgender inmates.
A group of inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria filed a lawsuit last year after President Trump issued an executive order at the start of his second term that prohibited the use of federal funds for medical procedures or treatments for transgender inmates within the federal Bureau of Prisons system. On the heels of that directive, the bureau issued new guidance that prohibited staff from granting requests for clothing accommodations for those inmates and barred the use of federal dollars for medical interventions.
The Bureau of Prisons then issued a new policy in February that it said was independent of Mr. Trump's executive order. Under those rules, the agency would continue providing mental health services for inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria, but would not provide surgeries, hormone therapy or social accommodations, like chest binders, wigs or breast padding, to address gender dysphoria.
Lamberth agreed to block the new rules in June and ordered the Bureau of Prisons to continue providing medical treatments to transgender inmates. The judge ruled in part that the administration's new policy was "reverse engineered" to implement Mr. Trump's executive order. He then issued an order last month continuing to block enforcement of the rules.
The Justice Department appealed. Earlier this month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit declined to restore the policy while proceedings moved forward.
In its request for emergency relief to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration accused the district court of "substituting its own policy judgment for that of the agency." The Bureau of Prisons, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said, determined its policy on medical treatments for transgender inmates was "necessary to maintain institutional security," and he warned that the district court's decision "nullifies" that judgment.
Sauer said the lower court order "prevents the application of the Executive's chosen policy" on a broad basis.
